title: Plastics Companies Are Writing Lesson Plans. What Could Go Wrong?
gist: A Plastic Pollution Coalition report finds the plastics industry (SPE/Plastics Industry Association, Dow-backed American Association of Chemistry Teachers, Shell) has been supplying free K-12 lesson plans and programs like 'PlastiVan' (132,000+ students reached since 2011) that promote industry talking points and recycling as the fix while downplaying health/environmental harms, even though only 9% of plastics are actually recycled worldwide; the piece (via Grist/Climate Desk) frames this as a pattern shared with tobacco, junk food, pesticide, and fossil fuel industries exploiting underfunded schools.

themes.theme: Scale and mechanics of industry-sponsored plastics curricula

insights.claim: A new report from the nonprofit Plastic Pollution Coalition documents the plastics industry inserting its agenda into US K-12 classrooms via free or cheap lesson plans, worksheets, hands-on science experiments, and touring programs like 'PlastiVan,' which travels city to city teaching about 'the contribution plastics make to modern life.'
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete, named corporate-influence channel (free curricula distribution) into a captive audience of 54 million K-12 students, a durable brand/reputation-shaping mechanism regulators or advocacy campaigns could target.
insights.quote: the contribution plastics make to modern life
insights.locator: para 2-3, on the Plastic Pollution Coalition report

insights.claim: The Society of Plastics Engineers (SPE), now a division of the Plastics Industry Association, runs lesson plans including a 'plastic scavenger hunt' aimed at teaching students plastics are ubiquitous and important to society, plus a video called 'Your Bottle Means Jobs' that frames plastics recycling as a local-employment driver.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Shows a trade association's direct branding presence in curricula, a specific case study for anyone tracking industry-association lobbying-adjacent activity beyond traditional government lobbying spend.
insights.quote: understand that plastics are ubiquitous and their importance to society and their personal life

insights.claim: The American Association of Chemistry Teachers, an initiative of Dow Chemical Company, distributes a lesson plan where elementary and middle school students compare plastic bag strength and are then asked to 'pretend' they are a Dow Chemical employee designing a plastic bag for a customer.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: A single-company (Dow) branded roleplay embedded directly in STEM curricula is a concrete example of brand-building starting in elementary school, relevant to ESG/reputation-risk screens on Dow.
insights.quote: pretend [they] are an employee for Dow Chemical Company
insights.locator: para 6, on the Dow-backed AACT lesson plan

insights.claim: Materials in the report claim STEM-standard alignment but, according to a National Center for Science Education specialist, fail to specify which state standards they meet or how, while padding lessons with industry jargon like 'stretch blow molding' and 'thermosetting' to create the appearance of rigorous science.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Documents a specific pedagogical red flag (jargon without standards alignment) that education buyers, school boards, or ESG researchers could use as a screening checklist for industry-sponsored STEM content generally, not just plastics.
insights.quote: By using all of these technical terms, it's tricking people into thinking … that they're doing science.

insights.claim: According to Wendy Johnson, the actual content taught by these plastics materials is 'ideological perspectives about the economy,' such as the desirability of cheap consumer goods, rather than genuine science education, and the purpose is to plant industry talking points rather than to teach.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Frames the curricula as messaging/influence infrastructure rather than education, useful for anyone modeling long-horizon consumer-sentiment or regulatory-tolerance shifts toward plastics.
insights.quote: It's so clear that the purpose isn't to make really clear, easy-to-use materials. The idea isn't to teach.
insights.locator: quote from Wendy Johnson on materials' true purpose

insights.claim: Some industry lesson materials acknowledge plastic pollution as a real problem but attribute it to irresponsible consumer behavior and push more recycling as the primary solution, rather than recommending reduced plastic production.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Identifies the specific rhetorical move (individualize blame, promote recycling, avoid production limits) that shapes public and possibly regulatory framing of plastics policy — relevant to handicapping the odds of production caps versus recycling-mandate-only regulation.

insights.claim: Only 9 percent of all plastics are recycled worldwide, and scientists have repeatedly warned that recycling capacity cannot keep pace with projected growth in plastic production, while investigative reporting has shown industry groups knew this decades ago yet promoted recycling anyway to defuse public concern over plastic pollution.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: A hard, citable data point (9% global recycling rate) plus a documented historical intent (defusing concern, not solving the problem) that materially undercuts the 'recycling solves it' narrative embedded in the curricula — a durable talking point for ESG and litigation risk analysis on plastics producers.
insights.locator: para 9, on the 9% global plastics recycling rate

themes.theme: Corporate community capture near petrochemical facilities

insights.claim: The Plastic Pollution Coalition report finds the propaganda problem is particularly acute in schools located near petrochemical facilities, and documents such industry activity in schools dating back to at least the 2000s.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Suggests a targeted, geographically concentrated influence strategy near production sites — a pattern investors tracking petrochemical community/regulatory relations (permitting, expansion approval) should watch for.
insights.locator: para 15, on proximity to petrochemical facilities

insights.claim: Between 2009 and 2011, a plastics trade group lobbied the California Department of Education to add a section titled 'The Advantages of Shopping Bags' to the state's high school textbooks, and SPE's PlastiVan program, running since 2011, claims to have reached over 132,000 students total.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete, dated precedent (2009-2011 textbook lobbying) and a scale metric (132,000+ students) for measuring the reach and persistence of this influence channel over 15+ years.
insights.locator: para 15, on 2009-2011 California textbook lobbying and PlastiVan reach

insights.claim: In Beaver County, Pennsylvania, Shell operates a 386-acre plastics production complex and has invested millions of dollars in plastics-related curricula and recycling programs for both grade schoolers and community college students, and has also donated backpacks of school supplies and funded a school basketball court, seemingly in exchange for incorporating plastics recycling into the curriculum.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: A named, quantifiable corporate-community investment (386-acre complex, millions in curricula funding, direct school gifts) tied to a specific facility — a concrete case study of a petrochemical company using local philanthropy to shape community and educational messaging around its own operations.
insights.locator: para 16, on Shell's Beaver County plastics complex and school donations

insights.claim: Shell, SPE, the American Association of Chemistry Teachers, and the Beaver County school district all did not respond to requests for comment from Grist.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Non-response from all four named parties is itself a signal of reputational sensitivity around this specific reporting, relevant to gauging how contested/actionable the underlying report's claims are seen to be by the parties named.
insights.locator: para 17, on non-response from named organizations

themes.theme: Underfunded schools as the structural vulnerability, and competing remedies

insights.claim: Teachers often lack the time and money to design their own curricula or buy high-quality materials for labs and science projects, which creates an opening that vested interests (tobacco, junk food, pesticide, or fossil fuel industries, not just plastics) have historically exploited by offering free instructional support.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Frames school underfunding as the root structural cause enabling industry curricular capture across multiple sectors, implying the fix (better school funding) is a policy lever distinct from banning any single industry's materials.
insights.locator: para 19-20, on the broader STEM funding gap

insights.claim: Madison Dennis of Plastic Pollution Coalition recommends school boards adopt policies banning educational materials sponsored by the chemical, fossil fuel, and plastics industries, and separately calls for eliminating tax breaks for petrochemical processing and plastics production facilities, arguing this would free up cash for communities and reduce dependence on industry-provided materials.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Names a specific, actionable policy ask (eliminate petrochemical tax breaks) that, if adopted at scale, would directly raise the effective cost/tax burden on plastics and petrochemical producers — a regulatory-risk signal to monitor at the state/local level.

insights.claim: Katie Allen of Algalita pushed back against blanket bans on industry-sponsored content, arguing teachers should be trusted to contextualize industry materials and could even use them to teach critical-thinking skills, framing outright bans as a slippery slope.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Represents a genuine internal disagreement among environmental educators/nonprofits over remedy design (ban vs. teacher discretion), meaning the 'ban sponsored content' policy push is not unanimous even within the advocacy community.
insights.quote: Once you start banning one thing, where does it end? What I want to do is give educators the benefit of the doubt and allow them to make their own decisions.

insights.claim: Nonindustry alternatives exist and are already in use: Algalita offers free lesson plans on ocean plastic garbage patches and biomagnification, and The Story of Stuff offers a broader high school curriculum on the costs and consequences of consumer goods production, including plastics.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Identifies specific nonprofit competitors already positioned to fill the curricular gap if industry-sponsored materials are restricted, relevant for anyone mapping the education-content supply chain around plastics/environmental topics.

insights.claim: A recently retired Berkeley elementary teacher, Jacqueline Omania, independently designed her own zero-waste curriculum starting in 2015, having her students develop annual zero-waste classroom agreements and campaign for a Berkeley policy requiring restaurants to stop giving out single-use plastic foodware.
insights.speaker: Joseph Winters
insights.so_what: Shows a bottom-up, teacher-driven alternative model that also produced real local policy change (a restaurant single-use-foodware rule), illustrating that grassroots curricula can translate into municipal regulation independent of industry or large nonprofit involvement.
insights.quote: There are so many challenges in the world, but plastic is something tangible. It's right there in front of them, and they can see the difference that they're actually making through their actions.
insights.locator: quote from Jacqueline Omania, closing anecdote
